title: Expressivity and Statistical Trade-offs in Diffusion Policy Learning

paper.title: Expressivity and Statistical Trade-offs in Diffusion Policy Learning
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion-based policies have recently emerged as powerful policy parameterizations for reinforcement learning, representing state-conditioned action distributions as terminal laws of diffusion processes with parameterized drifts. This terminal-law representation has shown substantial expressive flexibility in practice, enabling diffusion policies to model complex, multimodal, and highly non-Gaussian action distributions; however, it remains unclear what mathematically drives this expressivity and how to fully exploit it when the policy is learned from finite data.
In this paper, we identify the drift Lipschitz budget K K as a central quantity governing the expressivity and statistical behavior of diffusion policies. We quantify expressivity through approximation: diffusion policies with K K -Lipschitz drifts can concentrate near optimal deterministic policies and achieve value approximation error of order 1 / K 1/K ; moreover, we prove a matching lower bound under nondegenerate diffusion noise. This increased expressivity comes with a statistical cost. When the drift is parameterized by neural networks, increasing K K improves approximation but increases statistical complexity. Balancing these two terms yields a finite-sample performance gap of order 𝒪 ~ ( n − 2 / ( m + 6 ) ) \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-2/(m+6)}) for generic neural-network drifts, and a sharper rate 𝒪 ~ ( n − 2 / ( m + 4 ) ) \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-2/(m+4)}) for one-sided dissipative drift classes, where n n is the sample size and m m is the dimension of the state space. Numerical experiments provide empirical evidence for the sample-dependent trade-off in K K , supporting both theoretical regimes. Our framework also suggests a practical implementation principle: choose the diffusion budget K K according to the available sample size, and then select a neural-network architecture with the corresponding fixed Lipschitz coefficient.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Many reinforcement learning (RL) problems concern learning a stochastic policy that optimizes an expected objective through repeated interaction with the environment [ 58 ] . Policy-gradient and its variants are among the most widely used approaches for this task [ 20 , 29 , 51 , 52 , 59 ] . Their performance, however, depends critically on the choice of policy parameterization. An effective policy class must satisfy three requirements: (i) it should be expressive enough to approximate good, or even optimal, policies; (ii) it should allow efficient sampling of actions during interaction with the environment; and (iii) it should support tractable likelihood evaluation for constructing policy-gradient estimators (e.g., [ 59 ] ). Designing such policy classes becomes especially challenging beyond finite action spaces. In continuous-action RL, classical methods often rely on tractable stochastic policy families, such as Gaussian, Beta, Gaussian-mixture, or exponential-family policies, because these distributions are easy to sample from and have tractable likelihoods [ 20 , 22 , 51 , 52 ] . This computational convenience, however, comes with limited expressivity. Gaussian policies may be poorly matched to bounded or constrained action spaces, log-concave families cannot represent many multimodal action distributions, and mixture models can introduce numerical and optimization difficulties. As a result, these simple policy classes can struggle to represent the complex, multimodal, or strongly non-Gaussian action distributions that arise in modern RL tasks, such as multi-stage manipulation [ 12 , 33 , 49 ] and locomotion [ 27 ] . Diffusion-based policies provide a more expressive alternative by representing state-conditioned action distributions as terminal laws of diffusion processes with parameterized drifts. The key idea is to transform a simple reference distribution into a complex action law through stochastic dynamics. This approach has shown strong expressive power in generative modeling, including image and video generation [ 24 , 54 , 55 ] . Building on these advances, recent works have used diffusion models as policy parameterizations in control and RL [ 3 , 12 , 14 , 33 , 41 , 46 , 47 , 49 , 63 ] . These methods represent the action distribution at each state through a parameterized diffusion process. This allows the policy to capture rich and potentially multimodal action distributions that are difficult to express with standard policy families, while still allowing actions to be sampled by simulating the diffusion process. Despite this empirical success, the theoretical understanding of diffusion-based policies in RL remains limited. Existing theory for diffusion models mainly focuses on generative modeling and does not directly explain what drives the expressivity of diffusion policies for decision-making objectives. In particular, it remains unclear which structural quantity controls their ability to approximate optimal policies, and how to fully exploit this expressive power when the policy is learned from finite data. This leads to two fundamental questions: 1. Expressivity of diffusion policies : What mathematically governs the ability of diffusion policies to approximate optimal policies for a given RL objective? 2. Impact on learning and statistical guarantees: How does the increased expressivity of diffusion policies affect the finite-sample statistical error of policy learning? Answering these questions is challenging because the expressivity of diffusion policies is not merely a qualitative property of the representation. It depends on the Markov decision process (MDP) structure, the regularity of the optimal policy, and the quantitative complexity of the diffusion dynamics. Moreover, increasing expressivity may improve approximation while enlarging the statistical complexity of the learned policy class. This calls for a finite-sample theory that identifies the structural quantity driving expressivity and quantifies its role in the resulting approximation–estimation trade-off.

sections.heading: 1.1 Our contributions
sections.text: In this paper, we identify the drift Lipschitz budget K K as a central quantity governing the expressivity and statistical behavior of diffusion policies. We consider diffusion policies defined by state-conditioned stochastic differential equations with parameterized drifts and given volatility, and measure the complexity of the policy class through the drift Lipschitz constant K K . Our main contributions are four-fold. First, we establish the expressivity of diffusion policies through a sharp K K -dependent approximation theory. We prove that diffusion policies with K K -Lipschitz drifts can approximate deterministic optimal policies as K → ∞ K\rightarrow\infty , with mean-squared localization error of order 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / K ) \mathcal{O}(1/K) (Lemma 3.1 ). We then show that this rate is optimal and cannot be improved in general under nondegenerate diffusion noise (Proposition 3.3 ). We further translate these localization results into upper and lower bounds for RL value-function approximation, namely Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 3.4 . Second, we show that this increased expressivity comes with a statistical cost when the drift is parameterized by ReLU neural networks. For a generic K K -Lipschitz neural drift class, the learned policy error is bounded by three terms: diffusion approximation 1 / K 1/K , neural-network realization error s − 2 / m s^{-2/m} , and statistical estimation error s ​ K / n \sqrt{sK/n} , where s s is the network class size, n n is the sample size, and m m is the state dimension. Balancing these terms yields a value gap of order 𝒪 ~ ( n − 2 / ( m + 6 ) ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-2/(m+6)}) (Theorem 4.2 ). We further show that, if the neural drift class satisfies a one-sided dissipativity condition, the stability estimate improves and the statistical term becomes s / n \sqrt{s/n} , up to logarithmic factors. This gives the sharper rate 𝒪 ~ ( n − 2 / ( m + 4 ) ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-2/(m+4)}) ; see Remark 4.2 . In both regimes, these rates are achieved by choosing the diffusion budget K K depend properly on the sample size n n . Third, we derive a policy-gradient formula for continuous-time diffusion policies. Since the policy is defined implicitly as the terminal law of a diffusion process, its log-density function (also known as the score function) is generally not analytically tractable. We show that the score function can be substituted with a pathwise quantity derived from the diffusion process via Girsanov’s theorem. This yields a tractable policy-gradient expression in terms of the drift sensitivity (Proposition 5.2 ), and provides the training identity used in our numerical experiments. Fourth, we validate the two statistical regimes through numerical experiments. The first experiment trains a generic neural drift using our policy-gradient estimator in a nonlinear multi-step MDP setting. It illustrates the generic sample-dependent scaling K ≍ n 2 / ( m + 6 ) K\asymp n^{2/(m+6)} . The second experiment uses a mean-reverting, hence dissipative, diffusion-policy class in a controlled contextual bandit setting. It isolates the approximation and estimation terms and illustrates the sharper scaling K ≍ ( n / log ⁡ n ) 2 / ( m + 4 ) K\asymp(n/\log n)^{2/(m+4)} . Together, the experiments provide empirical evidence for the sample-dependent role of K K , and suggest a practical implementation principle: choose the diffusion budget K K according to the available sample size and then a K K -Lipschitz neural drift class.

sections.heading: 1.2 Related literature
sections.text: Our work is connected to several strands of literature on diffusion models, RL, and continuous-time stochastic analysis. The most closely related line studies diffusion models as flexible policy parameterizations for continuous-action RL. We also discuss diffusion-based planning and imitation learning, theory of score-based generative models, and the approximation, statistical learning, and PDE/SDE tools used in our analysis.

sections.heading: Diffusion policy in RL.
sections.text: One line of work directly represents the policy by a conditional diffusion model and trains or optimizes the parameters of the diffusion model [ 14 , 18 , 41 , 46 , 47 , 63 , 64 , 65 ] . Recent extensions further develop likelihood-based on-policy diffusion policy optimization, continuous-time Q Q -score matching, and maximum-entropy diffusion-policy training via adjoint matching [ 15 , 26 , 60 ] . A second line uses diffusion models primarily as samplers, generating actions from a given intermediate policy while training a classical RL algorithm [ 7 , 8 , 11 , 22 , 39 , 42 ] . Both lines of work are largely empirical, but they consistently demonstrate the strong expressive power of diffusion policies on large-scale RL tasks. In contrast, we provide theoretical foundations for this empirical observation by studying how the diffusion Lipschitz budget controls both expressivity and finite-sample statistical error in diffusion policy learning. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first theoretical results of this kind in the literature.

sections.heading: Diffusion planning, trajectory diffusion, and diffusion imitation learning.
sections.text: Diffusion models have also been used as trajectory-level planners and sequence/action generators for offline decision making and robot imitation learning [ 28 , 1 , 38 , 12 , 33 , 49 , 27 , 3 ] . These works provide important empirical evidence that diffusion parameterizations can capture multimodal, high-dimensional, and temporally correlated behavior distributions. Our setting differs in that we study Markov diffusion policies through their one-step state-conditioned action laws and prove explicit expressivity and statistical trade-offs.

sections.heading: Theory of diffusion and score-based generative models.
sections.text: Our analysis is also related to the theory of diffusion and score-based generative models [ 54 , 55 , 24 , 56 , 61 , 13 , 37 , 10 , 9 ] . Existing theory in this area primarily studies sampling, score estimation, and distribution recovery. In contrast, we connect the diffusion drift budget to RL performance by showing that K K -Lipschitz diffusion policies achieve, and in general cannot improve upon, a 1 / K 1/K value-approximation rate near deterministic optima.

sections.heading: Neural-network approximation, statistical learning, and PDE/SDE tools.
sections.text: Finally, the finite-sample part of our work builds on neural-network approximation and statistical learning theory for ReLU networks [ 66 , 45 , 50 , 4 , 44 ] , while the continuous-time analysis uses tools from stochastic calculus, stochastic control, and parabolic PDE theory, including Girsanov transformations, Fokker–Planck smoothing, and density/lower-estimate arguments for uniformly elliptic diffusions [ 57 , 30 , 43 , 36 , 5 , 2 , 32 , 6 , 21 ] .

sections.heading: Flow-based policy parameterizations.
sections.text: A closely related recent direction replaces stochastic diffusion sampling by ODE or flow-based generative policies, motivated in part by faster sampling and more direct pathwise or likelihood-ratio training. This includes online flow policies, Q Q -guided flow optimization, offline-to-online flow matching, reversible likelihood-ratio methods, MeanFlow and rectified-flow policies, and reparameterization-gradient training [ 40 , 17 , 53 , 25 , 16 , 35 , 68 , 67 ] . These methods are complementary to ours: pathwise training typically relies on a differentiable critic or action-value gradient, while likelihood-ratio training for generic flow policies requires inversion and Jacobian control, or special reversible constructions. In contrast, our analysis focuses on SDE terminal-law diffusion policies and proves a K K -dependent approximation–estimation trade-off.

sections.heading: 1.3 Roadmap
sections.text: The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the RL setting, the diffusion-policy parameterization, and the assumptions used throughout. Section 3 develops the expressivity theory for diffusion policies with Lipschitz drifts, including the resulting upper and lower bounds for value-function approximation. Section 4 studies finite-sample learning when the drift is represented by ReLU neural networks, decomposing the error into diffusion approximation, neural-network realization, and statistical estimation terms. Section 6 presents the policy-gradient training framework and numerical experiments illustrating both finite-sample regimes: the generic n − 2 / ( m + 6 ) n^{-2/(m+6)} trade-off and the sharper dissipative n − 2 / ( m + 4 ) n^{-2/(m+4)} trade-off. Section 7 concludes with the main takeaways and limitations of the work. Throughout, ∥ ⋅ ∥ \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm on finite-dimensional vector spaces. sections.heading: 3 Expressivity of diffusion policy
sections.text: We now turn to the approximation power of diffusion policies. The goal of this section is to show how the drift Lipschitz budget K K controls their ability to concentrate near deterministic optimal actions, and how this translates into value-function approximation.

sections.heading: 3.2 Lower bound on value function approximation for K K -Lipschitz drifts
sections.text: The upper-bound result shows that a K K -Lipschitz mean-reverting drift can concentrate a diffusion policy near an optimal deterministic action with squared error of order 1 / K 1/K . We now show that this rate is intrinsic: under nondegenerate diffusion noise, no K K -Lipschitz drift can localize the terminal action around a finite set of target actions at a faster rate. Proposition 3.3 (Matching lower bound for finite-set localization) . Let 𝒵 = { z 1 , … , z J } ⊂ ℝ d \mathcal{Z}=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{J}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} be a finite set and fix R > 0 R>0 . Let ( a ¯ t x ) t ≥ 0 (\bar{a}^{x}_{t})_{t\geq 0} follow ( 2.3 ), with a ¯ 0 x \bar{a}^{x}_{0} independent of B B . We give a few remarks about Proposition 3.3 . (i) Role of bounded volatility. For state-independent volatility, uniform ellipticity is enough. For state-dependent volatility, the upper bound in Assumption 2.1 is essential: Proposition A.5 shows that, if this upper bound is removed, the 1 / K 1/K lower bound can fail even when the volatility remains uniformly elliptic from below. (ii) Sharpness. The lower bound matches the 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / K ) \mathcal{O}(1/K) upper bound from the mean-reverting construction in Lemma 3.1 . Indeed, with finite second moment initialization and uniformly bounded volatility, a linear mean-reverting drift can achieve 𝔼 ​ ‖ a ¯ T − z ‖ 2 ≲ K − 1 \mathbb{E}\|\bar{a}_{T}-z\|^{2}\lesssim K^{-1} for any fixed z ∈ ℝ d z\in\mathbb{R}^{d} , and hence also 𝔼 ⁡ [ 𝖽𝗂𝗌𝗍 ​ ( a ¯ T , 𝒵 ) 2 ] ≲ K − 1 \mathbb{E}[{\sf dist}(\bar{a}_{T},\mathcal{Z})^{2}]\lesssim K^{-1} for any finite set 𝒵 \mathcal{Z} . The only additional assumption is that the Bellman gap grows at least quadratically locally near the finite set of optimal actions. Theorem 3.4 (Finite-well diffusion lower bound) . For each K ≥ 1 K\geq 1 and T > 0 T>0 , let π K , T \pi_{K,T} be the Markov policy whose action law at state x x is the terminal law at time T T of ( 2.3 ). Condition ( 3.4 ) is a mild finite-well condition on the Bellman gap. The clipping makes the assumption local in nature: near A ⋆ ​ ( x ) A^{\star}(x) , it requires the Bellman gap to grow at least quadratically with the distance to the optimal action set, while away from A ⋆ ​ ( x ) A^{\star}(x) , it only requires a positive suboptimality margin. sections.heading: 6 Numerical experiments
sections.text: Using the policy-gradient expression specified in Proposition 5.2 , we provide two numerical studies illustrating the two finite-sample regimes identified in Section 4 . The first experiment uses a generic neural drift class in a nonlinear multi-step MDP. This corresponds to Theorem 4.2 , where the leading statistical term contains the extra K K -factor and the optimal diffusion budget scales as K ≍ n 2 / ( m + 6 ) K\asymp n^{2/(m+6)} . The second experiment uses a mean-reverting, one-sided dissipative diffusion class. This corresponds to Remark 4.2 , where we first choose s = s ⁡ ( n ) ≍ ( n / log ⁡ n ) m / ( m + 4 ) s=s(n)\asymp(n/\log n)^{m/(m+4)} and then study the effect of varying K K .

sections.heading: 6.2 Experiment with dissipative drifts
sections.text: In this section, we consider a simpler setting of one-step contextual bandit and parameterie the drift in the dissipative regime described in Remark 4.2 . Here the policy uses a mean-reverting diffusion around a learned center, so the drift is one-sided dissipative in the action variable. We first choose s ⁡ ( n ) ≍ ( n / log ⁡ n ) m / ( m + 4 ) s(n)\asymp\big({n}/{\log n}\big)^{m/(m+4)} and hold this center-class size fixed while varying K K . We mark K ¯ \underline{K} as the smallest value of K K for which the diffusion error is comparable to the center estimation error. Beyond this point, increasing K K gives little further improvement in policy regret. Results. Figure 2 (a) shows that, for each fixed sample size, the learned policy gap decreases monotonically with K K and approaches the corresponding direct center-MSE plateau. The plateaus decrease as n n increases because a larger sample size supports a more accurate fitted center. In particular, unlike the generic neural-drift experiment, there is no U-shaped dependence on K K in this dissipative experiment. Figure 2 (b) shows that the direct center MSE decreases consistently with the theoretical guide ( n / log n ) − 2 / ( m + 4 ) (n/\log n)^{-2/(m+4)} . This is the approximation–estimation trade-off that determines s ⁡ ( n ) s(n) , and it is independent of K K . Figure 2 (c) shows the behavior at n = 512 n=512 . The diffusion error around the fitted center decreases with K K , while the direct center MSE remains constant because the same center h ^ n \widehat{h}_{n} is used for every K K . Consequently, the policy regret decreases toward the center-estimation floor. The marked K ¯ \underline{K} is the smallest diffusion scale for which the diffusion term is comparable to this floor; taking a larger K K does not improve the leading statistical rate. Panel (a) shows that the learned gaps decrease with K K toward the sample-dependent direct center-MSE plateaus, indicated by the dotted lines. Panel (b) compares the direct center MSE with the scaled rate ( n / log n ) − 2 / ( m + 4 ) (n/\log n)^{-2/(m+4)} . Panel (c) compares the policy regret, diffusion error around the fitted center, and direct center MSE at n = 512 n=512 ; the dashed line marks K ¯ \underline{K} , the smallest diffusion scale at which the diffusion error becomes comparable to the center MSE. (Markers show averages over five independent repetitions, and error bars indicate standard errors.) Overall, the two experiments illustrate distinct roles of K K . In the generic neural-drift regime, increasing K K improves expressivity but also increases statistical and optimization difficulty, producing a U-shaped trade-off. In the dissipative regime, the additional mean-reverting structure stabilizes the policy class: once s = s ⁡ ( n ) s=s(n) is fixed, increasing K K mainly reduces the diffusion error until the policy regret reaches the center-estimation floor. Thus K ≍ ( n / log ⁡ n ) 2 / ( m + 4 ) K\asymp(n/\log n)^{2/(m+4)} is a minimum sufficient scale under this additional structure, not an optimizer for a generic drift class. In general neural implementations, such dissipativity would need to be enforced through projection of the parameters which may be computationally expensive; in the toy numerical example of Section 6.2 , it holds by construction.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We develop a theoretical framework for understanding the expressivity and finite-sample behavior of diffusion policies in reinforcement learning. Our results show that the drift Lipschitz budget K K controls a fundamental approximation–estimation trade-off: larger K K improves diffusion approximation, but also increases the statistical complexity of learning. For ReLU drift classes, this yields an explicit finite-sample oracle inequality and a sample-dependent choice of K K , supported qualitatively by our numerical experiments. This work opens several directions for further study. One interesting question is whether the finite-sample bound in Section 4 can be sharpened using Bernstein-type concentration, under stronger variance or stability assumptions. It would also be valuable to incorporate optimization error from practical policy-gradient training.

The goal is to show that, after rescaling the last time interval of length K − 1 K^{-1} , the residual diffusion has an endpoint density uniformly bounded from above. sections.heading: A.4 Proof of Proposition 3.3 , Assumption (A2): state-independent volatility
sections.text: We first prove the matching localization lower bound in the simpler case where the volatility is state-independent. The proof separates two regimes: short horizon, where the K K -Lipschitz drift cannot concentrate an absolutely continuous initialization too quickly, and longer horizons, where the final K − 1 K^{-1} -length time window yields an inevitable K − 1 / 2 K^{-1/2} -scale fluctuation. sections.text: We next translate the finite-set localization lower bound into an RL value lower bound. The only additional ingredient is the quadratic finite-well Bellman-gap condition, which converts squared distance from optimal action set into loss in value. Proof. By Proposition 3.3 , applied for each cardinality J = 1 , … , M J=1,\ldots,M , there exist constants c J , R > 0 c_{J,R}>0 and K J , R < ∞ K_{J,R}<\infty such that the clipped finite-set localization lower bound holds for every finite set A ⊂ ℝ d A\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with | A | = m |A|=m . Then, for every finite set A ⊂ ℝ d A\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} with 1 ≤ | A | ≤ M 1\leq|A|\leq M , every admissible K K -Lipschitz drift, every admissible volatility satisfying the ellipticity bounds, and every terminal time T > 0 T>0 , 𝔼 ⁡ [ dist ⁡ ( a ¯ T , A ) 2 ∧ R 2 ] ≥ c M , R K , K ≥ K 0 . \mathbb{E}\left[\operatorname{dist}(\bar{a}_{T},A)^{2}\wedge R^{2}\right]\geq\frac{c_{M,R}}{K},\qquad K\geq K_{0}. sections.heading: A.6 Analog of Theorem 3.4 with arbitrary initialization
sections.text: The previous lower bound uses the absolute continuity of the initial distribution to control very short horizons. This subsection explains why the statement fails for arbitrary, possibly discrete, initialization. And then we show that the lower bound is restored once a burn-in time of order K − 1 K^{-1} is imposed.

sections.heading: A.6.1 Counterexample with discrete initialization
sections.text: Indeed, consider a diffusion from source a ¯ 0 = 0 \bar{a}_{0}=0 to the target distribution δ 1 \delta_{1} (point mass at 1 1 ). Let f ⁡ ( t , a , x ) = M f(t,a,x)=M constant for all a , t a,t and x x , so that a ¯ t = M ​ t + B t \bar{a}_{t}=Mt+B_{t} At time t = 1 / M t=1/M , we have a ¯ t ∼ N ⁡ ( 1 , 1 / M ) \bar{a}_{t}\sim N(1,1/M) , and hence 𝔼 ​ | a ¯ t − 1 | 2 = 1 / M → 0 \mathbb{E}|\bar{a}_{t}-1|^{2}=1/M\rightarrow 0 . The drift is constant in a a , hence K K -Lipschitz for every K K . Thus no lower bound uniform over all t > 0 t>0 can hold for arbitrary initialization. The obstruction is that the time horizon can be arbitrarily small, so the accumulated diffusion variance vanishes, while the drift magnitude is not controlled by the Lipschitz budget.

sections.heading: Appendix C Proof for Section 5
sections.text: This appendix proves the policy-gradient formula used in Section 6 . The argument first represents the diffusion policy through a reference driftless diffusion and a Girsanov change of measure, then differentiates expectations with respect to the drift parameter, and finally inserts this derivative into the standard performance-difference identity for discounted MDPs.

text: Expressivity and Statistical Trade-offs in Diffusion Policy Learning Skip to main content Report GitHub Issue × Title: Content selection saved. Describe the issue below: Description: Why HTML? Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2607.07967v1 [stat.ML] 08 Jul 2026 Expressivity and Statistical Trade-offs in Diffusion Policy Learning Viet Vu † † thanks: Stanford University, Emails: vietvu01@stanford.edu and renyuanxu@stanford.edu Renyuan Xu * Jiacheng Zhang † † thanks: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Email: jiachengzhang@cuhk.edu.hk Yufei Zhang † † thanks: Imperial College London, Email: yufei.zhang@imperial.ac.uk August 24, 2026 Abstract Diffusion-based policies have recently emerged as powerful policy parameterizations for reinforcement learning, representing state-conditioned action distributions as terminal laws of diffusion processes with parameterized drifts. This terminal-law representation has shown substantial expressive flexibility in practice, enabling diffusion policies to model complex, multimodal, and highly non-Gaussian action distributions; however, it remains unclear what mathematically drives this expressivity and how to fully exploit it when the policy is learned from finite data. In this paper, we identify the drift Lipschitz budget K K as a central quantity governing the expressivity and statistical behavior of diffusion policies. We quantify expressivity through approximation: diffusion policies with K K -Lipschitz drifts can concentrate near optimal deterministic policies and achieve value approximation error of order 1 / K 1/K ; moreover, we prove a matching lower bound under nondegenerate diffusion noise. This increased expressivity comes with a statistical cost. When the drift is parameterized by neural networks, increasing K K improves approximation but increases statistical complexity. Balancing these two terms yields a finite-sample performance gap of order 𝒪 ~ ( n − 2 / ( m + 6 ) ) \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-2/(m+6)}) for generic neural-network drifts, and a sharper rate 𝒪 ~ ( n − 2 / ( m + 4 ) ) \tilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-2/(m+4)}) for one-sided dissipative drift classes, where n n is the sample size and m m is the dimension of the state space. Numerical experiments provide empirical evidence for the sample-dependent trade-off in K K , supporting both theoretical regimes. Our framework also suggests a practical implementation principle: choose the diffusion budget K K according to the available sample size, and then select a neural-network architecture with the corresponding fixed Lipschitz coefficient. 1 Introduction Many reinforcement learning (RL) problems concern learning a stochastic policy that optimizes an expected objective through repeated interaction with the environment [ 58 ] . Policy-gradient and its variants are among the most widely used approaches for this task [ 20 , 29 , 51 , 52 , 59 ] . Their performance, however, depends critically on the choice of policy parameterization. An effective policy class must satisfy three requirements: (i) it should be expressive enough to approximate good, or even optimal, policies; (ii) it should allow efficient sampling of actions during interaction with the environment; and (iii) it should support tractable likelihood evaluation for constructing policy-gradient estimators (e.g., [ 59 ] ). Designing such policy classes becomes especially challenging beyond finite action spaces. In continuous-action RL, classical methods often rely on tractable stochastic policy families, such as Gaussian, Beta, Gaussian-mixture, or exponential-family policies, because these distributions are easy to sample from and have tractable likelihoods [ 20 , 22 , 51 , 52 ] . This computational convenience, however, comes with limited expressivity. Gaussian policies may be poorly matched to bounded or constrained action spaces, log-concave families cannot represent many multimodal action distributions, and mixture models can introduce numerical and optimization difficulties. As a result, these simple policy classes can struggle to represent the complex, multimodal, or strongly non-Gaussian action distributions that arise in modern RL tasks, such as multi-stage manipulation [ 12 , 33 , 49 ] and locomotion [ 27 ] . Diffusion-based policies provide a more expressive alternative by representing state-conditioned action distributions as terminal laws of diffusion processes with parameterized drifts. The key idea is to transform a simple reference distribution into a complex action law through stochastic dynamics. This approach has shown strong expressive power in generative modeling, including image and video generation [ 24 , 54 , 55 ] . Building on these advances, recent works have used diffusion models as policy parameterizations in control and RL [ 3 , 12 , 14 , 33 , 41 , 46 , 47 , 49 , 63 ] . These methods represent the action distribution at each state through a parameterized diffusion process. This allows the policy to capture rich and potentially multimodal action distributions that are difficult to express with standard policy families, while still allowing actions to be sampled by simulating the diffusion process. Despite this empirical success, the theoretical understanding of diffusion-based policies in RL remains limited. Existing theory for diffusion models mainly focuses on generative modeling and does not directly explain what drives the expressivity of diffusion policies for decision-making objectives. In particular, it remains unclear which structural quantity controls their ability to approximate optimal policies, and how to fully exploit this expressive power when the policy is learned from finite data. This leads to two fundamental questions: 1. Expressivity of diffusion policies : What mathematically governs the ability of diffusion policies to approximate optimal policies for a given RL objective? 2. Impact on learning and statistical guarantees: How does the increased expressivity of diffusion policies affect the finite-sample statistical error of policy learning? Answering these questions is challenging because the expressivity of diffusion policies is not merely a qualitative property of the representation. It depends on the Markov decision process (MDP) structure, the regularity of the optimal policy, and the quantitative complexity of the diffusion dynamics. Moreover, increasing expressivity may improve approximation while enlarging the statistical complexity of the learned policy class. This calls for a finite-sample theory that identifies the structural quantity driving expressivity and quantifies its role in the resulting approximation–estimation trade-off. 1.1 Our contributions In this paper, we identify the drift Lipschitz budget K K as a central quantity governing the expressivity and statistical behavior of diffusion policies. We consider diffusion policies defined by state-conditioned stochastic differential equations with parameterized drifts and given volatility, and measure the complexity of the policy class through the drift Lipschitz constant K K . Our main contributions are four-fold. First, we establish the expressivity of diffusion policies through a sharp K K -dependent approximation theory. We prove that diffusion policies with K K -Lipschitz drifts can approximate deterministic optimal policies as K → ∞ K\rightarrow\infty , with mean-squared localization error of order 𝒪 ⁡ ( 1 / K ) \mathcal{O}(1/K) (Lemma 3.1 ). We then show that this rate is optimal and cannot be improved in general under nondegenerate diffusion noise (Proposition 3.3 ). We further translate these localization results into upper and lower bounds for RL value-function approximation, namely Theorem 3.2 and Theorem 3.4 . Second, we show that this increased expressivity comes with a statistical cost when the drift is parameterized by ReLU neural networks. For a generic K K -Lipschitz neural drift class, the learned policy error is bounded by three terms: diffusion approximation 1 / K 1/K , neural-network realization error s − 2 / m s^{-2/m} , and statistical estimation error s ​ K / n \sqrt{sK/n} , where s s is the network class size, n n is the sample size, and m m is the state dimension. Balancing these terms yields a value gap of order 𝒪 ~ ( n − 2 / ( m + 6 ) ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-2/(m+6)}) (Theorem 4.2 ). We further show that, if the neural drift class satisfies a one-sided dissipativity condition, the stability estimate improves and the statistical term becomes s / n \sqrt{s/n} , up to logarithmic factors. This gives the sharper rate 𝒪 ~ ( n − 2 / ( m + 4 ) ) \widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n^{-2/(m+4)}) ; see Remark 4.2 . In both regimes, these rates are achieved by choosing the diffusion budget K K depend properly on the sample size n n . Third, we derive a policy-gradient formula for continuous-time diffusion policies. Since the policy is defined implicitly as the terminal law of a diffusion process, its log-density function (also known as the score function) is generally not analytically tractable. We show that the score function can be substituted with a pathwise quantity derived from the diffusion process via Girsanov’s theorem. This yields a tractable policy-gradient expression in terms of the drift sensitivity (Proposition 5.2 ), and provides the training identity used in our numerical experiments. Fourth, we validate the two statistical regimes through numerical experiments. The first experiment trains a generic neural drift using our policy-gradient estimator in a nonlinear multi-step MDP setting. It illustrates the generic sample-dependent scaling K ≍ n 2 / ( m + 6 ) K\asymp n^{2/(m+6)} . The second experiment uses a mean-reverting, hence dissipative, diffusion-policy class in a controlled contextual bandit setting. It isolates the approximation and estimation terms and illustrates the sharper scaling K ≍ ( n / log ⁡ n ) 2 / ( m + 4 ) K\asymp(n/\log n)^{2/(m+4)} . Together, the experiments provide empirical evidence for the sample-dependent role of K K , and suggest a practical implementation principle: choose the diffusion budget K K according to the available sample size and then a K K -Lipschitz neural drift class. 1.2 Related literature Our work is connected to several strands of literature on diffusion models, RL, and continuous-time stochastic analysis. The most closely related line studies diffusion models as flexible policy parameterizations for continuous-action RL. We also discuss diffusion-based planning and imitation learning, theory of score-based generative models, and the approximation, statistical learning, and PDE/SDE tools used in our analysis. Diffusion policy in RL. One line of work directly represents the policy by a conditional diffusion model and trains or optimizes the parameters of the diffusion model [ 14 , 18 , 41 , 46 , 47 , 63 , 64 , 65 ] . Recent extensions further develop likelihood-based on-policy diffusion policy optimization, continuous-time Q Q -score matching, and maximum-entropy diffusion-policy training via adjoint matching [ 15 , 26 , 60 ] . A second line uses diffusion models primarily as samplers, generating actions from a given intermediate policy while training a classical RL algorithm [ 7 , 8 , 11 , 22 , 39 , 42 ] . Both lines of work are largely empirical, but they consistently demonstrate the strong expressive power of diffusion policies on large-scale RL tasks. In contrast, we provide theoretical foundations for this empirical observation by studying how the diffusion Lipschitz budget controls both expressivity and finite-sample statistical error in diffusion policy learning. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first theoretical results of this kind in the literature. Diffusion planning, trajectory diffusion, and diffusion imitation learning. Diffusion models have also been used as trajectory-level planners and sequence/action generators for offline decision making and robot imitation learning [ 28 , 1 , 38 , 12 , 33 , 49 , 27 , 3 ] . These works provide important empirical evidence that diffusion parameterizations can capture multimodal, high-dimensional, and temporally correlated behavior distributions. Our setting differs in that we study Markov diffusion policies through their one-step state-conditioned action laws and prove explicit expressivity and statistical trade-offs. Theory of diffusion and score-based generative models. Our analysis is also related to the theory of diffusion and score-based generative models [ 54 , 55 , 24 , 56 , 61 , 13 , 37 , 10 , 9 ] . Existing theory in this area primarily studies sampling, score estimation, and distribution recovery. In contrast, we connect the diffusion drift budget to RL performance by showing that K K -Lipschitz diffusion policies achieve, and in general cannot improve upon, a 1 / K 1/K value-approximation rate near deterministic optima. Neural-network approximation, statistical learning, and PDE/SDE tools. Finally, the finite-sample part of our work builds on neural-network approximation and statistical learning theory for ReLU networks [ 66 , 45 , 50 , 4 , 44 ] , while the continuous-time analysis uses tools from stochastic calculus, stochastic control, and parabolic PDE theory, including Girsanov transformations, Fokker–Planck smoothing, and density/lower-estimate arguments for uniformly elliptic diffusions [ 57 , 30 , 43 , 36 , 5 , 2 , 32 , 6 , 21 ] . Flow-based policy parameterizations. A closely related recent direction replaces stochastic diffusion sampling by ODE or flow-based generative policies, motivated in part by faster sampling and more direct pathwise or likelihood-ratio training. This includes online flow policies, Q Q -guided flow optimization, offline-to-online flow matching, reversible likelihood-ratio methods, MeanFlow and rectified-flow policies, and reparameterization-gradient training [ 40 , 17 , 53 , 25 , 16 , 35 , 68 , 67 ] . These methods are complementary to ours: pathwise training typically relies on a differentiable critic or action-value gradient, while likelihood-ratio training for generic flow policies requires inversion and Jacobian control, or special reversible constructions. In contrast, our analysis focuses on SDE terminal-law diffusion policies and proves a K K -dependent approximation–estimation trade-off. 1.3 Roadmap The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the RL setting, the diffusion-policy parameterization, and the assumptions used throughout. Section 3 develops the expressivity theory for diffusion policies with Lipschitz drifts, including the resulting upper and lower bounds for value-function approximation. Section 4 studies finite-sample learning when the drift is represented by ReLU neural networks, decomposing the error into diffusion approximation, neural-network realization, and statistical estimation terms. Section 6 presents the policy-gradient training framework and numerical experiments illustrating both finite-sample regimes: the generic n − 2 / ( m + 6 ) n^{-2/(m+6)} trade-off and the sharper dissipative n − 2 / ( m + 4 ) n^{-2/(m+4)} trade-off. Section 7 concludes with the main takeaways and limitations of the work. Throughout, ∥ ⋅ ∥ \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm on finite-dimensional vector spaces. For a map h : E → ℝ q h:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{q} , we define ‖ h ‖ ∞ := sup x ∈ E ‖ h ⁡ ( x ) ‖ \|h\|_{\infty}:=\sup_{x\in E}\|h(x)\| and Lip ⁡ ( h ) := sup x ≠ x ′ ‖ h ⁡ ( x ) − h ⁡ ( x ′ ) ‖ / ‖ x − x ′ ‖ \operatorname{Lip}(h):=\sup_{x\neq x^{\prime}}\|h(x)-h(x^{\prime})\|/\|x-x^{\prime}\| . We use ∥ ⋅ ∥ op \|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}} and ∥ ⋅ ∥ HS \|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{HS}} for the operator and Hilbert–Schmidt norms, respectively, and ∥ ⋅ ∥ L p \|\cdot\|_{L^{p}} for function-space L p L^{p} norms.
